## What exists now

The "recipe book" (right column of `InventoryPanel.tsx`) is a **single flat scrolling list of every recipe** — 45 base crafting recipes at the table, plus furnace/villager recipes that swap in when you're at those stations. Each row is `ingredient icons → result icon`. There's **no grouping, no labels, no search, no sorting**. Recipes you can't afford or that need a station are just dimmed in place.

Two things make that list hard to scan:
- **It's long** — ~45 rows at the base table.
- **It's repetitive** — 7 tiers each of pickaxe / sword / spear = 21 near-identical rows, so the things you're hunting for blur together.

## My opinion: yes, grouping is worth doing

A few reasons it's a genuine win and low-risk here:
- The data **already carries the grouping signal** — every result item has a `kind` (`block | weapon | tool | armor | food | material`) in `lib/game/items.ts`. So categories can be *derived*, not hand-maintained, which means they can't drift out of sync with the recipes.
- `recipes.ts` is **already loosely ordered by category** in source (the comments literally say "Building & materials / Tools / Weapons / Ranged & endgame / Armor / Food & smelting") — grouping just makes that structure visible instead of implicit.
- It's **faithful to Minecraft** — the modern MC recipe book has category tabs (equipment / building / misc / food), so this isn't a foreign concept; if anything the current flat list is the less-Minecrafty version.

The main caveat: at the furnace and villager the list is already filtered to one station, so grouping mostly pays off in the **base crafting-table view**. That's fine — that's where the 45 rows live.

Craft a **wood door** from **6 planks** and place it on a solid floor with two

# Gameplay Reference

Scannable tables for everything in the game: recipes, blocks, mobs, and item
stats. For how it all fits together, read the [player manual](manual.md).

> **The code is the source of truth.** These tables are a convenience snapshot of
> `lib/game/recipes.ts`, `lib/game/items.ts`, `lib/world/blocks.ts`,
> `lib/game/mobs.ts`, and `lib/game/mobLoot.ts`. If a number here disagrees with
> the game, the code wins — and this page needs an update.

## World types

Chosen when you create a world (alongside the name and seed) and fixed for its
life. All four share the same five biomes — they reshape terrain, not the biome
mix. Source: `lib/world/worldTypes.ts` + `terrainConfigFor` in `lib/world/generation.ts`.

| Type      | Terrain                                                                                     |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Default   | Balanced terrain with every biome — the original generator                                  |
| Superflat | Level ground at a fixed height; a builder's canvas (caves and ores still generate below)    |
| Amplified | Exaggerated relief — towering peaks and deep valleys                                        |
| Islands   | A raised sea breaks the land into scattered, gently sloped islands with deep ocean channels |

## Recipes

**54 crafting recipes** (plus **10 villager trades**, listed under [Trading](#trading)).
All use the always-available crafting grid except the nine **furnace** smelting
recipes, which need an open furnace.

| 2 Glass     | 4 Sand               |

| 1 Furnace   | 8 Cobble             |

A **profile** (name + skin) owns a list of named **worlds**, like user accounts on a shared console — pick a profile, then pick or create a world to play. All client-side in localStorage; **zero new assets** (the menus reuse the existing Minecraft-style chrome and generated skin portraits)
27	  - **Two-level save hierarchy** (`lib/game/profiles.ts`, `lib/game/worlds.ts`): a versioned `minecraft_profiles_v1` manifest (`{ id, name, skinId, createdAt }` + `activeProfileId`) and a `minecraft_worlds_v1` index (`{ id, profileId, name, seed, worldgenVersion, createdAt, lastPlayedAt }`), with each world's `SaveData` in its own `minecraft_world_save_<id>` key. New-world seeds are resolved once at creation (blank → random, numeric → clamped, other text → stable FNV hash). The skin moved off the old global `minecraft_skin_v1` key onto the profile; **audio settings stay global**
28	  - **Menu shell** (`components/GameShell.tsx`, `components/menu/*`): a profile-select → world-select → play state machine with create / rename / delete on both levels (deleting a profile cascades its worlds and their save blobs). The tab remembers its active world in `sessionStorage`, so a reload resumes straight back into play while a fresh tab cold-starts at the menu. The pause menu gains **Save & Quit to Worlds**
29	  - **Per-world worldgen versioning**: each world records the `WORLDGEN_VERSION` it was generated under (`lib/game/config.ts`). A future worldgen change bumps that constant and discards only the affected worlds' stale block-diffs (rebooting them from their seed) — replacing the old whole-store `SAVE_KEY` rename, which reset every world. The save _schema_ is unchanged (still version 5)
30	  - **First run & migration** (`lib/game/legacyMigration.ts`): a brand-new player is greeted by the create-profile form (name + skin) — their first act is making a profile. An existing single-world save is instead folded into a default "Player" profile (carrying the old skin) plus one "My World"; the legacy blob is copied before the old key is removed, so a failure can't lose data
31

35	
36	- Starting play now requires a double-click to acquire pointer lock, preventing an accidental single click from immediately capturing the mouse. No save-format or worldgen impact.
37	- Emergency unstuck now requires **`Shift` + `U`** instead of a bare `U`, so a stray keypress can no longer teleport the player mid-play. The automatic unstuck safeguard (which fires when wedged in terrain or falling below the world) is unchanged. No save-format or worldgen impact.
38	- Placed glass now renders as a clear, low-reflection transparent layer. Internal faces between adjacent glass blocks are culled, while neighboring opaque block faces remain visible through it. No save-format or worldgen impact.

## Summary

The crafting recipe book was one long, unlabeled scroll of every recipe — ~64 rows at the base table once dimmed furnace/villager recipes are counted, and heavy with near-identical tiered tools/weapons (7 each of pickaxe/sword/spear), so finding a recipe meant scanning the whole list.

This groups recipes into **labeled sections** with the recipes you can make **right now** floated to the top of each group:

- **Tools, Weapons, Armor, Building, Food, Materials** — derived from each result item's existing `kind`
- **Smelting, Trades** — station-gated recipes (furnace / villager) grouped by station so they stay together rather than scattering across the kind groups

Categories are *derived* from existing data, so they can't drift out of sync and adding a recipe needs no extra metadata. It's pure UI presentation — **no save-format, worldgen, or recipe-data change**.

EOF
)"
